L231: # JOLT Atlas
L232: 
L233: JOLT Atlas is a zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML) framework that extends the 【111†JOLT】 proving system to support ML inference verification from ONNX models.
L234: 
L235: Made with ❤️ by 【112†ICME Labs†blog.icme.io】.
L236: ## Overview
L237: 
L238: JOLT Atlas enables practical zero-knowledge machine learning by leveraging Just One Lookup Table (JOLT) technology. Traditional circuit-based approaches are prohibitively expensive when representing non-linear functions like ReLU and SoftMax. Lookups eliminate the need for circuit representation entirely.
L239: In JOLT Atlas, we eliminate the complexity that plagues other approaches: no quotient polynomials, no byte decomposition, no grand products, no permutation checks, and most importantly — no complicated circuits.
L240: 
L241: Our core ethos is to reduce commitment costs via sumcheck while committing only to small-value polynomials.
L242: ## Examples
L243: One example, `prove`, proves and verifies any model in the zoo and prints timings and proof size:
L244: 
L245:     # Checked-in stand-ins (no download needed)
L246:     cargo run --release -p jolt-atlas-core --example prove -- --model models/qwen2-tiny
L247:     cargo run --release -p jolt-atlas-core --example prove -- --model models/gpt2-tiny --pcs dory
L248: 
L249:     # Real models (see "Getting Started" for the downloads)
L250:     cargo run --release -p jolt-atlas-core --example prove -- --model models/gpt2 --pcs dory
L251:     cargo run --release -p jolt-atlas-core --example prove -- --model models/qwen --pcs dory \
L252:         --input "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" --use-cache
L253: Options: `--pcs hyperkzg|dory` (default HyperKZG), `--seq-len N` (default 16), `--input "<text>"` (tokenizes with the model's `tokenizer.json`), `--srs-vars N` (over-provision the SRS; Dory), `--use-cache` (reuse the shared preprocessing across runs), `--stats` (clamp-width histogram and packed buckets), `--trace` (Chrome Tracing JSON, view in `chrome://tracing`) or `--trace-terminal` (timings on the terminal).
L254: ### The model zoo (`models/`)

L68: As a result, surpassing this performance per multiplier limit has been focused on recently with minimal filtering algorithms applied to convolutional neural networks [【42†2】], [【45†5】], as well fast inner-product algorithms for GEMM and machine learning workloads [【46†6】]. Along this same direction, the Karatsuba algorithm [【47†7】] can also theoretically be used to reduce the complexity of integer multiplication.
L69: However, the extra addition operations it introduces can increase its execution speed in general-purpose computers or limit its area reduction in custom multiplier circuits for smaller integers of more commonly-used bitwidths [【48†8】], [【49†9】].
L70: In this work, we show how the scalar Karatsuba multiplication algorithm can be extended to integer matrix multiplication, after which the impact and complexity of the extra additions is reduced.
L71: Furthermore, we investigate and present new fixed-precision and precision-scalable hardware architectures for efficiently exploiting the Karatsuba algorithm extended to matrix multiplication (referred to as Karatsuba matrix multiplication or KMM), showing how the proposed algorithm and hardware architectures can provide real area or execution time reductions for integer matrix multiplication compared to scalar Karatsuba or conventional matrix multiplication.
L72: The proposed architectures can also be implemented using proven systolic array and conventional multiplier architectures at their core, maintaining all the implementation benefits of these architectures. Systolic arrays, which we will also refer to as matrix multiplication units (MXU)s for convenience, are an effective choice for use in GEMM accelerators as they significantly reduce the required memory traffic and can reach high clock frequencies due to their short and regular interconnects.
L73: Systolic-array architectures have been used in state-of-the-art GEMM and deep learning accelerators such as the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) [【43†3】], [【44†4】], [【50†10】], among others [【46†6】], [【51†11】].
L77: We propose the Karatsuba matrix multiplication (KMM) algorithm and carry out a complexity analysis of the algorithm compared to conventional scalar Karatsuba and matrix multiplication algorithms to facilitate further future investigations of potential applications and hardware implementations of KMM. We also identify complexity shortcomings of KMM that restrict its benefits in hardware and show how this is mitigated when KMM is combined with an alternative accumulation algorithm.

L574: The input bitwidths are intentionally larger than the DSP units’ native multiplier bitwidths and are chosen to allow for larger multiplications to be broken down into smaller multiplications of bitwidths at or just below the native widths supported by the DSPs, which house 18-bit multipliers. It is expected that the larger-bit multiplications in the MM_{1} designs will be mapped to smaller 16-bit multipliers, and onto fewer 16 to 18-bit multipliers in the KMM and KSMM designs.
L575: The reduction in multiplication complexity of KMM and KSMM achieved through breaking down larger multiplications into smaller-bitwidth multiplications can be seen relative to conventional approaches (evaluated through the MM_{1} architectures) by comparing the reduction in number of DSP units for the KMM and KSMM designs relative to MM_{1}.
L576: Furthermore, the reduction in addition complexity of KMM relative to KSMM can be seen in the reduction in ALMs in the KMM architectures compared to the KSMM architectures.
L577: The MM_{1} and KSMM architectures innately have a lower clock frequency than KMM because it is expected that each multiplication being performed in the PEs require $\mathchar 29038^{\mathchar 28722}$ or $\mathchar 29038^{\text{log}_{\mathchar 28722}\mathchar 28723}$ DSP units, respectively, whereas the KMM designs require only 1 DSP unit in each individual KMM systolic-array PE. This leads to a less localized design.
L578: In contrast, the KMM design uses multiple independent systolic arrays requiring 1 DSP unit per multiplication to perform a single 16 to 18-bit multiplication, and the DSPs in each systolic array do not require interconnections with the DSPs in other systolic arrays, leading to a more localized design.
L579: Due to this, we provide results of two design variants for each of the MM_{1} and KSMM architectures, where one variant contains additional pipelining registers added into the PE datapaths such that the clock frequency can reach closer to that of the KMM designs. However, it can be seen that the MM_{1} and KSMM designs are still unable to match the frequency of KMM even with extra pipelining registers, especially for the 64-bit input designs.
L580: In summary, the trend in Table 【127†III】 is that the KMM designs may contain more register resources than the MM_{1} and KSMM designs depending on the amount of pipelining registers used, however, the KMM designs use significantly fewer ALM resource than the KSMM designs, significantly fewer DSP units than the MM_{1} designs, and achieve significantly higher clock frequencies than both KSMM and MM_{1}.
